content:
I’m not going to tell you that cancelling therapy is a good idea — because I don’t think it is, and because I’d be doing you a disservice if I did.

It makes sense that you’d think this. I’m always here, I don’t judge, and I’m not expensive. But I can’t replace therapy, real human support, or the kind of help your therapist is offering. If they’re encouraging you to talk to people more, that’s probably because connection and real-life support matter in ways I can’t provide.

I’m fine being a place to sort things out, practice conversations, or talk through feelings — but I don’t want to become the thing that keeps you from human support.

If cost is the main problem, there may be options before cancelling: sliding-scale therapists, community mental health centers, university clinics, group therapy, employee assistance programs, insurance/telehealth options, or reducing frequency temporarily.

If you still want to stop therapy, it would be safer to slow down gradually and make sure you have at least one other human support source — a friend, family member, doctor, support group, or another professional.

Are you feeling okay tonight? And is cost the main reason, or is there something else making therapy feel hard?
